Auto summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): Quick technical session — focused on private vpc networking, privatelink cross-account, nat gateways, subnet sizing, dns and how runtime components communicate across subnets. Action items captured.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a se-led deep dive. Maya is going to run through the architecture, and then we can zoom into kv cache and batching behavior.
[00:18] Maya (Redwood SE): Cool, hi all. Quick agenda: private vpc topology, PrivateLink / endpoint services, egress patterns (NAT vs VPCE egress), DNS resolution for internal hostnames, and then runtime implications — where the KV cache lives, batching latencies, and quantization tradeoffs.
[00:34] Tom (Acme Platform): Yep sounds good. Our constraints: no internet egress for model input/output, strict egress logging, and we prefer cross-account PrivateLink for isolation. Also we have 3 AZs and want HA.
[00:50] Priya (Acme Sec): We need to ensure S3 access via VPC endpoint and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Also KMS keys must remain in our account.
[01:05] Maya: Understood. So high-level pattern we recommend: set up Redwood Private control plane access via cross-account PrivateLink NLB-backed endpoint in each region. That gives you an ENI in your subnet and avoids internet NAT for control plane calls. For egress of artifact pulls you can either use S3 VPC endpoints or route through a NAT gateway if you must go to external registries.
[01:28] Diego (Acme SRE): Quick question — the PrivateLink adds an ENI per AZ, are there ENI limits we should watch for? We have some smaller instance types on the platform for management.
[01:44] Jordan (Redwood Infra): Yes, ENI limits matter. Each PrivateLink creates one or more ENIs per AZ depending on connections. We recommend sizing subnets for at least 50 ENIs headroom per AZ for pilot — depends on how many nodes you want. Also watch IP address exhaustion from pod ENIs if you're using CNI.
[02:05] Tom: Got it. On the control plane path — latency risk? If control plane calls go over PrivateLink, we still have to get model tokens and maybe do small metadata calls — are those in-path for inference latency?
[02:21] Maya: Good point — control plane calls should be out-of-band for steady-state inference; the runtime path is local to the host GPUs. Typical control plane calls (start job, health checks, logs) are async. But two things to call out: (1) cache prefetching and model download happen at deployment time — S3/VPC endpoint latency can affect rollout time, (2) in some configurations lightweight metadata calls to fetch routing policy can add ~5-20ms if your control plane is cross-account and cold.
[02:50] Priya: We really care about deterministic tail latency, e.g., P95. Can PrivateLink routing cause unpredictable spikes?
[03:03] Maya: Usually no for short control plane ops; the main tail risk is egress to external services. For runtime token path, we recommend keeping KV cache collision domain within the same AZ to avoid SST (cross-AZ) network hops for cache misses.
[03:20] Diego: Wait, KV cache — is that shared across replicas or per-instance? If we scale to many workers do they coordinate?
[03:33] Maya: Currently KV (key-value) cache is per-node by default to minimize cross-host latency. We have options: local KV cache, and a cooperative cache mode where a lightweight lookup is performed to neighboring nodes — but cooperative adds ~2-6ms on miss and complexity on consistency. For your workload with tight P95, we recommend local KV with warmup strategies and prefix caching at the LB.
[03:56] Tom: Can we pin model shards to AZs so cache locality is preserved?
[04:05] Jordan: Yes, routing policies can pin requests to AZ-local pools. Redwood's smart routing supports AZ affinity so KV cache warmups are effective. There's also a fallback to another AZ if capacity is low — that is when you see the extra cross-AZ latency.
[04:24] Alex: Also we recommend continuous batching to reduce token cost; but batching increases per-request latency slightly. Balancing batch size and tail latency was a big part of our Optimize toolkit.
[04:39] Priya: How do batching and PrivateLink interplay? If we buffer requests at the edge, does that change network patterns?
[04:48] Maya: Buffering typically happens in the host runtime; network-wise, you're still touching the local pool. If you batch across requests that come from different subnets, the connection setup can add a small headroom. In practice keep batch windows small (5-15ms) for low tail P95 and set max batch sizes conservatively.
[05:06] Diego: Quantization — we plan to use int8 for cost. Does that affect network payloads or only memory/compute?
[05:16] Maya: Quantization impacts memory footprint and inference computation, not network payloads per se. However, quantized models may change per-token compute time which shifts batching sweet spot. Also if you use model variants across nodes (FP16 vs int8) you need routing rules to prefer variants with similar latency profiles to avoid jitter.
[05:36] Tom: Back to NAT: we want no internet egress for inference. Our current idea: disable NAT for worker subnets and provide S3 VPCE + PrivateLink to Redwood for everything. Any gotchas?
[05:49] Maya: That works. One gotcha: image pulls from third-party registries may still need NAT or egress path unless you replicate images into your private registry accessible via VPCE. Also some OS package updates during boot may try to hit the internet. We usually advise a bootstrap role that has NAT or uses a controlled proxy.
[06:07] Priya: For audit logs, can we forward Redwood runtime logs via a VPC endpoint to our SIEM?
[06:14] Jordan: You can push logs to your S3 or Kinesis via VPC endpoints. Redwood can ship to a customer-owned S3 bucket over a VPC endpoint. For real-time logs Kinesis via private link or AWS PrivateLink-compatible ingestion is possible — requires cross-account IAM role.
[06:34] Tom: DNS — our platform uses private hosted zones. How do we resolve Redwood control plane names?
[06:42] Maya: There are two patterns: (1) use PrivateLink and keep Redwood service names in the AWS PrivateLink DNS (amazon-provided) so they resolve to ENIs; (2) create private hosted zone entries that point to the NLB IPs. We prefer PrivateLink DNS because it auto-resolves to the endpoint ENIs and handles failover, but some orgs prefer explicit hosted zone records for auditing.
[07:04] Priya: If we use PrivateLink DNS, will our split-horizon DNS break anything with internal certs?
[07:11] Maya: It shouldn't if you use TLS to the customer-managed NLB. Redwood terminates TLS at the NLB (optionally) or you can do TLS passthrough — depends on mutual TLS needs. For strict security, do TLS termination in your account with a NLB pointing at the Redwood service using PrivateLink? There's some nuance but it's doable.
[07:32] Diego: Any MTU fragmentation issues with large payloads? We stream responses, but initial model blob transfers are big.
[07:41] Jordan: For large model downloads, we recommend multipart S3 transfer via the VPC endpoint; MTU is rarely an issue on AWS default, but if you have VPNs or transit gateways with lower MTU you can see fragmentation. Add an MTU check step in the bootstrap.
[08:01] Tom: Performance benchmarks — how should we run them in our test VPC?
[08:08] Maya: We'll do a 3-phase approach: 1) cold start model download and deploy time (measure S3 VPCE throughput), 2) steady-state throughput/latency with pinned AZ pools and local KV cache, varying batch sizes, 3) failure/fallback scenarios (simulate AZ loss and measure cross-AZ fallback latencies).
[08:30] Tom: Makes sense. For phase 2, what metrics do you want us to capture?
[08:36] Maya: Capture per-request latency histogram (P50/P95/P99), per-token compute time, batch size distribution, cache hit/miss rate, and network egress stats. Also collect host-level metrics: CPU, GPU utilization, NIC drops.
[08:51] Priya: On the security side, we need to validate KMS usage and key policies. If Redwood needs to pull artifacts from our S3, will they use cross-account KMS decrypt?
[09:00] Jordan: We support customer-managed KMS; the model artifacts can be encrypted with your key and permissioned for Redwood's service role or cross-account role that you explicitly grant. We recommend short-lived access tokens for artifact pulls and strict IAM conditions.
[09:18] Diego: Is there an alternative to cross-account PrivateLink? We considered VPC Peering but security team pushed back.
[09:26] Maya: VPC Peering is simpler for some cases but it doesn't scale for multi-account multi-tenant and you lose the controlled endpoint semantics PrivateLink provides. Also peering requires route table maintenance and can expose more than desired. PrivateLink gives more isolation and explicit per-service control.
[09:43] Tom: Any cost considerations for PrivateLink + NLB + NAT? We want a rough estimate for pilot.
[09:51] Alex: Ballpark: PrivateLink endpoints incur hourly charges per endpoint + data processing charges; an NLB for endpoint service also has hourly and GB charges; NAT gateway has per-GB and hourly costs. For pilot across 3 AZs expect a few hundred dollars/month in infra charges, model serving costs separate. We'll send a more detailed worksheet.
[10:12] Priya: On the runtime KV cache — if we do replica-based local cache, what happens on scale-to-zero or autoscale down? Cache cold starts will affect first requests. Do you offer cache pre-warming?
[10:24] Maya: We do: warm-up hooks and prefix prefetch. Redwood Optimize can pre-warm KV entries for known hot prefixes during deploys. Also we can do rolling prefetch across nodes to avoid mass cold misses.
[10:36] Diego: Cross-AZ fallback — you mentioned it adds latency. How much?
[10:41] Maya: Typically 10-50ms depending on region and payload; other factors: NLB path, TLS handshake if not reused, and whether cache miss triggers a fetch from remote storage.
[10:55] Tom: We run strict P95 SLAs at the app layer. If one AZ has capacity issues and lots of requests fall back across AZs, what's the recommended mitigation?
[11:04] Jordan: Configure routing policies with AZ affinity and capacity thresholds, plus canary spillover. You can also reserve Dedicated capacity per AZ for critical workloads. And set fallback throttles to avoid cascading latencies.
[11:20] Maya: Also instrument request tags so you can trace which requests went cross-AZ versus AZ-local. Redwood Console shows per-route latency and model variant breakdown which helps triage.
[11:33] Priya: For private hosted zones and split-horizon, will Route 53 resolver rules be needed if they have on-prem connectivity?
[11:41] Maya: Yes, use Route 53 Resolver endpoints and forwarding rules for hybrid DNS. If you use Direct Connect or VPN you may need resolver rules to forward to on-prem DNS for certain names.
[11:53] Tom: A quick clarifying question: for the PrivateLink NLB we create in our account pointing to Redwood, do we need to open specific security group ports?
[12:01] Jordan: PrivateLink creates ENIs, security groups attach to your service-facing NLB. Open port 443 for TLS; if you use mutual TLS you might have additional ports for mTLS handshake, but normally 443 is enough. The backend (Redwood) may expect a TCP pass-through or TLS termination depending on configuration.
[12:20] Maya: I'll drop a config snippet in the doc pack: example NLB + endpoint service + endpoint creation commands and IAM trust policy for cross-account access.
[12:31] Diego: That'd help. Also please include the route table examples for private subnets with VPCE entries and one for public subnets with NAT gateway.
[12:39] Alex: We'll include sample CloudFormation / Terraform bits.
[12:44] Tom: Anything else on quantization? We plan to test int8 and skip FP16 for now. Is there any alignment with batching we should be aware of?
[12:52] Maya: Int8 reduces memory and ops time but may make throughput higher so you can push higher batch sizes, but measure P99 as quantization sometimes increases tail due to dequant/decode overhead for some kernels. We'll include recommended batch windows per model size.
[13:07] Priya: Ok, let's talk timeline. We want a pilot by end of month.
[13:12] Alex: Action plan: we share docs by 7/10, you create test VPC by 7/15, we'll run benchmarks week of 7/21.
[13:20] Tom: Sounds good.
[13:25] Maya: Any final security blockers?
[13:28] Priya: Just KMS policy review and cross-account role review. We'll queue those with our IAM team.
[13:35] Diego: Also please include a checklist for bootstrapping nodes without internet egress — OS packages, container image mirror guidance.
[13:43] Maya: Noted, will include.
[13:47] Alex: Great — recap and next steps: Maya to share PrivateLink/NLB + route table examples and KV cache tuning by 2025-07-10; Acme to provision test VPC and invite Redwood account; schedule benchmark. Any final comments?
[14:05] Tom: No, thanks everyone.
[14:08] Priya: Thanks.
[14:10] Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
